Title: The Priory of the Orange Tree (The Roots of Chaos, #1)
Author: Samantha Shannon
My Review:
There’s so much going on that almost nothing really ends up happening. Characters jump around the world
like they’re travelling just to the corner store. People SWIM across boats like it is nothing. Stuff appears out of nowhere and the plot builds itself on a flimsy structure.
The last 15% were the worst as you can feel that there was a need to wrap up the story but seems like little thought was given to the end (dragons vs boats? a character swimming from one boat to another during a battle? characters teleporting? uber enemies dying like they were nothing to fuss about?)
Not everything is bad, as the scenes are beautifully built, and the love story is appropriate, but there’s so much going on that seems badly glued on! I’m glad that I read the book as a ebook because if it was a physical copy (which is a behemoth) this would have probably been a DNF!

Pros:
- at 1/2 of the book we get some backstory and lore of the world - this felt nice
- good description of new places; while they don’t feel necessarily alive, you can tell how beautiful they all are

Cons:
- the first 6 chapters are a bit of a mess for me; there are names, cultures, events, and more, thrown around that lack context - there’s so much room to explain stuff but that ends up not happening. I don’t feel like i should have to read 7+ chapters to understand the fundamental values of the a kingdom but that’s what happens
- the way characters traverse the map makes it feel very tiny - maybe the fault is comparing this to TLoTR, but the journeys that characters take feel meaningless
- i wish there was more lore along the book; there are a lot of names and stuff thrown at you but except for 2 moments, you learn very little about the world and its customs
- i don’t get the point of Niclays Roos other than to be there to give exposition to stuff we wouldn’t know of otherwise
- same way characters traverse the world and make it feel tiny, there are 2/3 instances where characters swim between boats or from/to beaches and they make it seem like that is nothing; it kinda ruins the immersion for me

My Review:

Title: Carrie
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
I usually write my review in Pros and Cons bullet points but there are no cons about this so full text will be.

King has an amazing ability to write gruesome scenes and make us doubt his own sanity; I’m sure he’s more than okay with that but it’s books like Carrie that make people give him a bad look. That’s how good the book is!

I’ve read Carrie after reading Cell and while the destruction vibe feels similar, it’s so much better achieved in Carrie. Cell felt very long, while the journey was obvious, but, Carrie… it was just the perfect length.

I don’t know how much King lived to be able to write the characters that he writes, but they feel so alive, so real, so disgustingly human, that the horror in them transpires so easily into us that you actually feel sorry and disgusted by and for them.

Anyway, I’m just rambling. It’s a very good book. The writing is amazing, the plot is good, the story is horrific, the details are disgusting, the emotions are raw.

It’s not for everybody (horror never is) and a lot of people will judge the story based on the acts of animalistic nature, but if you can look past that, you’ll get it

Title: Recursion
Author: Blake Crouch
My Review:
3.5⭐️ actually

I always end Crouch’s books feeling like they should actually be tv series. I guess that makes sense considering he’s seen as a screenwriter but I think that this approach works poorly for the second half of his books.

Recursion is a good book but if I’m reading the same thing 3-4 times, it just feels like … wasted time, I dunno.
Repeating stuff works great in television and there’s always a different way of showing stuff , but with writing… I jut don’t think it works

The first half of the book felt amazing; everything made sense, and although the pacing was a bit slow, I was enjoying the book.
The second half, tho… It felt very, very slow, and the impactful moments just got lost in the repetition and need to move forward to be able to wrap up the story.

Something was off. We followed the characters in several timelines and the climax is achieved by omitting an action of the sole character that we’re following how are we spending so many pages talking about each step the characters take but we then jump the part where Barry breaks into Slade’s house to remove the bullets???

The book went on for too long for its own good and that makes me sad

Title: Snow Crash
Author: Neal Stephenson
My Review:
I wasn’t expecting the book to be this awful, but it is.
There’s so much exposition / lore, given by one sided dialogue that it gets extremely boring and uninteresting!
The second half of the book is basically just one character explaining things to the other, with a “Oh yeah?” or “What do you mean?” in the middle just so you remember that there’s someone else in play.

I honestly don’t understand how this book has such a high rating considering the amount of info dump that it does.
The world is cool and the concept was fairly new at the time, but the characters are flat as a sheet of paper, and the dialogue is … something.
I don’t know what was the author’s reason to expose the world or plot like this but it reads like something a beginner would write.

Title: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
If you have the chance, hear the audiobook before reading the book, since you’ll hear the words from the King himself.

As a wannabe writer, On Writing is a kick in the balls; I’m 32, with no experience, and haven’t written more than 2 pages in the last 2 years, so King tells me “You’re not gonna make it” and he’s right. But maybe I also needed this message to be said loud and clear for me to get real about it.

As a reader, On Writing helps me understand what is and isn’t a good book; I don’t like how I end up describing a book as “something is off” and King’s explanations of what should be avoided made perfect sense to me (adverbs, long exposition, dialogue tags).

As a King enjoyer, knowing his process and life was very refreshing, which is made even better on the audiobook.

Title: A Fire Upon the Deep (Zones of Thought, #1)

My Review:

The journey part seemed to never end and there was A LOT of exposition
The plot also felt contrived at times and I’m not a fan of having a single character “saving the world”; the resolution of the menace also felt very weak.

I also feel like this book could have been maybe 3 different ones; or it could have been cut in half - there was no need for it to be so long in the uninteresting parts.

I’m sad for this; the book had an amazing way of talking about stuff: no long explanations about the whys because that’s just how it is, but then it lost itself on trying to find a solution for a problem it itself created

Title: Blood Meridian, or, the Evening Redness in the West
Author: Cormac McCarthy
My Review:
Blood Meridian is raw, harsh, poetic, long, boring, repetitive, detached, confusing, brave, glorious, epic and biblical.

I can’t get into meaningful discussions about the whys and hows of the book but I can say that my reading took me through all the feelings above.
As non-native English speaker, Blood Meridian was a hard book to read; the vocabulary and the flow of the phrases mean that it’s very easy for a person to call quits very early when trying. However, I persisted and I enjoyed it; I didn’t LOVE it because I feel like there’s a lot that I missed but I learned that at certain excerpts it was just better for me to ‘let go’ and let the story flow.

Anyway, it’s a good book. The characters aren’t particularly important nor is their journey. I feel like the main message could be summarised to a single phrase but I wouldn’t consider the length of the book unnecessary; for me it strengthened the meaning that I took from it.

Title: American Psycho
Author: Bret Easton Ellis
My Review:
Artistry is being able to look at something and being able to reshape it into something memorable, groundbreaking and iconic, and whomever did the movie for this book is an artist without a doubt because the book itself is absolutely horrible.

If you’ve watched the movie and are thinking to yourself “I want to know what the source material looks like”, I’ll save you the trouble:
- the iconic scenes from the movie resemble almost nothing to the book; and the movie does them soooooo much better
- unless you’re a fun of lists, info dump, and, particularly, snuff, this book will bore you, disgust you, and make you doubt of your economic decisions since you’ve actually had to pay to get the book
- the style and iconic brands from the movie are well present on the book but there’s only so many times that I can read “double breasted wool suit” without getting bored
- the violence in the book are borderline nonsensical and provide nothing to the story; they are, once again, provided in a list form and serve just as padding to the message of “hey, guys, he’s a real psycho, right?”
- you don’t feel the tilt and tense environment in the book as you do in the movie simply because each chapter in the book feel extremely detached from one another

So, yeah, you’re probably better off skipping this one

Title: A Game of Fear (Inspector Ian Rutledge, #24)
Author: Charles Todd
My Review:
This most likely on me for getting into a series with one of the most recent books, which means I don’t have the full context of the characters, but I can’t stop making comparisons to Peter Robinson’s Inspector Banks stories.
On those, the characters are always presented like it was the first time meeting them, which small details exposed that you didn’t get from other times; here, however, you’re jumping into the unknown and that means that I couldn’t connect with any of the characters.
Apart from that, the narrative didn’t fit me since the characters have no pause on them, a moment for the sense of them to settle.
It saddens me, because I wanted to like it, especially with so many good comments.

Title: Sputnik Sweetheart
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
This is, most likely, a me issue and not a Murakami issue but this is the last try I give to his work.
I just can’t get into it.
His stories always feel the same to me:
- a “love” triangle
- imposing erections
- rough sex scenes
- immature characters (even if they have 10+ years of difference between themselves)
- no explanation to the ‘fantastic realism’ that suddenly happens
- lacklustre ending

Again, maybe it’s me, but there always seems to lack focus in his stories, without a lot of ‘tell’ and very little of ‘show’

Title: May the Wolf Die
Author: Elizabeth Heider
My Review:
Good book, with a good story and Simon Vance does, once again, a good job narrating the book (if it wasn't for his way of narrating I probably wouldn't have picked up the book, if I'm being honest).
Near the end, the book started edging towards the 3⭐ since I felt like the closure and finale weren't on part with the rest of the story

Title: The Dancer at the Gai-Moulin (Maigret #10)
Author: Georges Simenon
My Review:
Maigret acts like a superstar in this one and I’m here for it.
Also, Simenon has a marvellous way of storytelling and it’s refreshing to find one of the stories with Maigret not being the main character for the first half

Title: Maigret e o crime no Far-West
Author: Georges Simenon
My Review:
The best Maigret is the observant Maigret and since we find him here in the US, all he can do is, indeed, observe and think.
I think that Simenon does a marvelous job exposing the American way of living and the mysterious vibes that it has for an outsider that is used to a very different culture and way of doing things.
I can only advise this book to those who’ve read plenty of Maigret before because this is not a book of mystery or crime, but a book about Maigret’s personality and his way of doing and thinking about things

Title: Candide
Author: Voltaire
Additional Authors: Rockwell Kent, Walter Jerrold, Don Hagen, Sara Gioacchino Corcos
My Review: Funny, to a certain degree, but the “Look at this scenario where this poor fool finds himself” gets old very quickly. I enjoyed the final message of the book a lot more than the situations that it describes

Title: The Carter of 'La Providence' (Maigret, #2)
Author: Georges Simenon
My Review:
Coming from more recent books of Maigret’s stories, you can really tell that this one was done really at the start. It lacks Maguire’s personality in it but the scenery descriptions are amazing.
It’s interesting that you can see Simenon’s writing evolving and how Maigret is being shaped with each book.
The story was fine, but the narrative was confusing sometimes! There were a lot of jumps between places, one paragraph after another and it made the reading a bit chaotic.
In any case, it’s a fun read.

Title: Standing in the Shadows (Inspector Banks, #28)
Author: Peter    Robinson
My Review:
If not for Simon Vance, the narrator, I probably wouldn’t have picked up this book, but the sample I picked on Libby was enough.
The story is good. Banks is a cool cat and a good leader, with a well adjusted personality and worried look for the cases he gets. The plot is okay but the characters and reading, personally, were what made it shine for me.

Title: The Talented Mr. Ripley (Ripley, #1)
Author: Patricia Highsmith
My Review:
If you feel like reading a book where not a lot happens other than people travelling from one place to another, without as much as a fair description of the places, then this book is for you.
There’s a lot of ‘telling’ instead of ‘showing’ and the writing pivots itself between being warm and personal, and distant and plain
Even the character development of Tom is fairly poor; there’s no lesson to take from this first book.
The movie, in this case, is a lot better; if not for the story then for the visuals and the fashion

Title: The Terror
Author: Dan Simmons
My Review:
I think that the score of this book suffers from survivorship (no pun intended) bias! Most people would feel discouraged reading a real life events inspired store with more than 700 pages and that supposedly has terror notes in it.
I, for one, got it because it was at 0,99€; and why did I read it to the end? Honestly, no idea, I had no reason to suffer with it but I did so I could at least give it a score of finishing the book and not DNF!
Now, for the review:
1. The book is dramatically long and I don’t think that it has good reasons for it to be so; it has a lot of words and phrases but most of the times there aren’t really events in it, it just feel like a log - even where there’s jumps in time (like, let’s say, one chapter is on the 5th of June and the next one is on the 25th), the author goes back and basically exposes all the days anyway, making the timeline confusing (the chapter names have the name of the places, the coordinates, and the date)
2. There are too many characters, which made me care for absolutely none; worse than that, I couldn’t even remember what some of they were because they had not enough exposition for me to care
3. There’s a whole chapter that sounds like a Cirque du Soleil routine (I barely know ship parts and now I’m reading how there’s a person swinging from one place to another?)
4. The book is so ship-heavy, and I have so little understanding of ships, that most of the times I didn’t know what we were talking about; I understand that Dan did his research but I didn’t really need to pass that entirely to us
5. The first 60% of the book are incredibly dull and didn’t evoke any emotion to me; maybe it’s due to how it is exposed, or how we’re jumping from perspective, but I couldn’t care about the challenges of the people
6. The exploration part was interesting because stuff started happening very quickly, but, again, maybe it was just in contrast with the rest of the book
7. There’s nearly no ‘Terror’ in it as in ‘horror’; there’s an unpronounceable beast and people dying but, once again, the exposition of it didn’t feel good
8. We got relevant info presented in the last 5% of the book; who does that and why would I care now?
9. We spent a lot of time hyping the bad guys to get nearly nothing from it
10. Same thing with the beast

I’m still going to read Hyperion, but, please, Dan, don’t do this to me again!

Title: Fahrenheit 451
Author: Ray Bradbury
My Review:
For someone reading Fahrenheit 451 as their first dystopian book, I can see how it can greatly impact them, but once you widen your knowledge, you feel that its message is bleak and superficial.
The book reads like a badly structured poem, where the author seems to create a narrative that would sound good out loud but mean very little.
Also, the world is barely built; there are headphones and giant TVs but it is so awfully explained in the first encounters that you need some extra time to understand that the main character is actually describing real life and not just having an imaginative episode.
Overall, didn't enjoy it at all; I'm sad to feel like this about a book about books but it landed flat on me

"Bill, the Galactic Hero" just sounded dumb, but then I remembered that all great heroes have a noun and a title: "Bill, the Galactic Hero," "Rick, the Door Technician," "Thomas, the Tank Engine."

Title: The War of the Worlds
Author: H.G. Wells
My Review:
I appreciate what the book tries to do, especially to the time in which it was written, but I couldn’t connect with it.
Here are the flaws that it has, for me:
- the ‘report’ style of narrative feels old after a while, especially when we move from the main character’s POV to his brother’s, which means that we’re now on the realm of ‘someone told me that someone told him’ and that loses impact
- the book is very long for what it tries to convey and cutting it short could have being beneficial
- I absolutely disliked the jumps in time during the first week; I got lost with the events because we were jumping between 4 different days and couldn’t create a proper narrative in my mind

Title: Against A Dark Background
Author: Iain M. Banks
My Review:
What an amazing mess of a book! I wanted to enjoy it—I really did—but there's so much wrong with it.
Here's a list of what I definitely didn't enjoy:
- all the characters read as being edgy and snarky, with very brief moments of them actually feeling like humans
- each new setting dumps the system's specs (ecological, historical, geological, etc.), which would be fine if they weren't so damn long and out of context (it reads like it's trying to set the scene for a play)
- the plot is all over the place with so much going on, when in reality very little has to do with the story
- the most interesting parts are about Sharrow reminiscing about the past
- the last 1/5 of the book is spent on a magical uni-bike that solves literally everything!
- there's a multitude of bad guys that, in the end, makes them all feel incredibly weak and that they clearly don't know what they are doing
- this is a personal issue but ... in a time of spaceships and laser guns, somehow there's a part where people get lost in a jungle/fjord and nearly die from hunger?

This could have been three or four different books, each interesting in its own way (Sharrow's past, Sharrow's future, Sharrow's family, and the never-ending battle for Colter, just to name a few topics), but it fails miserably to do so.
The writing isn't bad and what kept me pushing to reading it was because I wanted to get invested in the story and the characters but the pages went on and the story got worse.

My Review:
If there's something that I didn't expect to ever do it's to read a play about robots. But it works!
It's a short read but powerful, with its message loud and clear, and it takes one of the prime stops for one of the better works illustrating 'the uprising of man-made stuff'

Title: The Death of Ivan Ilych
Author: Leo Tolstoy
My Review:
Had no expectations for the book but it is very good! I wholeheartedly recommend it to everybody.
It’s not a 5⭐️ simply because it doesn’t have a wow factor

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
Author: Gabriel García Márquez
My Review:
This book just wasn't for me...
The jumps in time, the interminable plot, the endless fantastical occurrences that exist and make you wonder if you missed something two pages back...
Overall, it felt incomplete for me. The path was there but there was no story around it, and I felt like I was reading through different milestones set for the plot to arrive to; there's so much going on that nothing matters.
In the end, it felt like I was reading a book by someone who read Tolkien (regarding the worldbuilding, story telling, and epic events) but that didn't want to go through the fantasy route and ended up very short of what was possible

My Review: Average, at most... If I didn't knew Nietzsche, this book surely wouldn't get me to read more of his stuff

One thing I found weird about the book was the decision to have Charlie narrate/write his reports. At a certain point, where he's at his 'intelligence climax', the 'report' feels like it no longer exists, but we're still getting a description of it as it does.

In any case, it's a wonderful book, from its cadence to its meaning to how the characters develop. I wholeheartedly recommend it to everybody!

Title: Remote: Office Not Required
Author: David Heinemeier Hansson
My Review:
The book might be losing its relevance by the day since each day more people get into contact with the notion of remote work, and, thus, the introduction to it that this book provides is not enough for a vast majority of people or scenarios.
That being said, it still deserves its praise for potentially being a good starting point to introduce the conversation into a company (assuming management is even interested in it)

Title: Cujo
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
Oof, extremely hard for me to rate this book and here’s why: the suspense scenes are incredible and King does, like always, an amazing job at creating people and having them have real issues.
But the book is so long with no apparent reason, just for the sake of building more unfortunate scenarios.
I liked it, but also hated it!

Title: Brave New World
Author: Aldous Huxley
My Review:
First 1/3 was incredible and the world setting felt good, but I feel like we built that world for nothing. No one was breaking out of it with a bang, we just saw someone that never belonged to it keeping that way.
The rest of the book was dull, long, jumping in the timeline, and out of character with the rest.
I’m all for moral and societal lessons but you can’t just throw the world you built away and focus solely on that

Title: Engine Summer
Author: John Crowley
My Review:
'Engine Summer' follows the narration of Rush-that-Speaks, a boy who lives in a settlement, located in space in a post-apocalyptic-event Earth, that, inspired by the stories of Earth's 'angels', leaves his home on a pilgrimage of self-enlightenment built on experienced and told stories. In his Path, Rush is faced with the myths and memories that shape his civilization and culture, reflecting on an outside world that is strange, hidden, and that does not always say what it means and means what it says.

What makes a good sci-fi book, for me, is the author's ability to immerse us in the world without worrying about explaining every small detail like we're newborns to it. This is not easy, and very often it's off-putting for a large crowd, but Crowley does it marvellously. 'Engine Summer' reads like a poem and dream, with the right cadence, description, and timeline. Leaning heavily on a love-journey type of plot ( for a girl and also for Rush's meaning of life ), we're taken into exploring a world that feels very familiar but very strange since it seems to have been frozen in time and has people fed in that still-image. 'Engine Summer' takes its time allowing Rush to explore this new-old world and know what is beyond Little Belair, his settlement.... Until the last 1/4, I mean, which is where the artistry is replaced by a rushing feeling of ending a journey and where the elegance and complicated apparent simplicity ends, feeling almost disconnected for the rest of the story.

If a layered world with a heavier layered meaning behind it calls for you, 'Engine Summer' won't disappoint you but you should be prepared to wander, aimlessly, in a strange world, with different groups living it differently.

My Review:
This short story wins a high ranking place in my heart from King’s amazing ability to build kids, how they think and how the world perceives them!
The style and writing in this story unlocked something for me, and I think it has the perfect mix of characters, plot, narrative and all the good stuff that makes King King!

Title: The Adventures of Amina al-Sirafi (Amina al-Sirafi, #1)
Author: Shannon Chakraborty
My Review:
This book deserves every kind of praise for Chakraborty’s research and use of bibliography. As an introduction to any type of Muslamic folklore (and maybe even the history), I enjoyed being ignorant of a lot of stuff written here so I could research them myself.
Now to the story itself…
At times, the book felt like a very good DnD campaign, but unfortunately the times where it felt disconnected and pathless were more often.
I think that the first 1/3 of the book is very good; it sets the plot in a good way, there are fun scenarios to explore and the details are on point. The second and last third, however, felt incrementally disconnected, losing the polished descriptions and events, and I was getting madly frustrated by it.
It pains me to give the book a ‘meh’ review but I just couldn’t get around to love it and enjoy it as it is. Come to think of it, it ended up feeling very YA

Title: The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo (Millennium, #1)
Author: Stieg Larsson
Stephen  King
My Review:
At points the story felt very lovecraftian, at others it just went full balls to the wall on the gore.
Most of the plot is interesting, even if it lasts for too long. Also, there is a chunk of the story that I felt tricked by due to the narration of events in which the character wasn’t present but still knew what happened. I would have preferred if the perspective had switched and then had the main character find out some other way instead of the ‘well, they told me that…’.
Anyway, good story, the audiobook is great

Title: Eversion
Author: Alastair Reynolds
My Review:
This is a good book! It didn’t left me in awe with it (probably because I was left confused with the different times but the plot is good, the characters are loveable enough and it’s a nice read.
There’s nothing inherently bad with it but I would like to have a bit more of context at the start of the chapters (maybe a year or something) so I could understand where I’m standing.
Now that I understand the entire plot, surely the second reading will be a lot better.
In any case, if you feel yourself confused and willing to give up the book, don’t! Eventually everything will make sense

Title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
Author: Philip K. Dick
My Review:
It has some pacing issues that threw me off, and the writing is average, but some sections of the book feel so immensely developed and try to convey such a large meaning that it completely makes up for it.
I like books that make me look for their meaning (which is most of the good SF, I guess) and this one is no different; it feels weird and murky at times but I take great joy in seeing people discussing the philosophical meaning of what PKD created here

Title: 2001: A Space Odyssey (Space Odyssey, #1)
Author: Arthur C. Clarke
My Review:
An interesting book but it just didn’t scratch the itch fully.
Since I never saw the movie, I wasn’t expecting it to be existentialist but I appreciated the change! I didn’t, however, find much SciFi in it (maybe the book is showing its age?).
In any case, it is definitely a good read

Title: Foundation (Foundation, #1)
Author: Isaac Asimov
My Review:
Asimov deserves all the praise for being one of the pioneers of SciFi, but this book, for me, just isn't showing that.
There's a lot of talk (maybe 95% of the book is just talking) and I just couldn't get into it. I didn't know what to attach myself to since:
1. the plot was somewhat interesting but even with time jumps it didn't develop
2. there's little to no world-building apart from the politics (which I understand why it gets a major focus)
3. the characters are constantly trying to one-up the others by showing how smart they are (I've never read the phrase 'Yeah, I know what you mean, you can skip that', or a derivative of it, so many times!)

Title: Sea of Rust (Sea of Rust, #1)
Author: C. Robert Cargill
My Review:
Aww, man… I wanted to like the book but it felt so anticlimactic and dull. The story felt extremely flat for me, and I wasn’t able to care for any of the characters.
Despite the fact that the book is about robots, and nearly solely with robots, they could have been replaced by something else completely and the story would land the same way
The world building felt nonexistent, the descriptions were mostly about fight scenes (which felt like 80% of the book) and the characters were flat as a sheet of paper.
It doesn’t get 2⭐️ because the idea was interesting and there are bits of reflection

The Body joins The Eyes of the Dragon and Fairy Tale as one of my favourites from Stephen King and my recommendation to anyone who wants an outrageously good book.
On paper, there is nothing interesting in the story's premise: 4 kids walk to see a body near the railroad and regular life events happen. BUT IT IS SOOOOO GOOD! King seems to have a special talent to create mundane characters that just live average lives and that ends up giving so much to his book. A group of friends, doing kid stuff, but having adolescent conversations that naturally appear during their age opens up the story to being so much more than a physical journey from point A to point B
---
About the audiobook, Frank Muller is an amazing narrator and I feel like he gave the twang necessary for the characters to feel even more alive!

Title: Lisey's Story
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
This is a very long boy, and I feel I could have lived without the repeated statement of the same stuff. It just felt, for me, unnecessarily long for what it encompassed.
The language in the book is also not easy to digest. There's so much made-up-in-between-members-of-a-couple and infant language that I just kept thinking about doggo. That's what reminded me of and it was off-putting. It's relatable (any couple will have made up words) but I just kept going back to thinking: doggo, and that's not the ideal word to think of when the author is trying to set the thriller mood.
All of this almost made me drop the book to 3⭐...

However...
It's a brilliant thriller! The mix between past and present (and maybe a bit of side-but-on-another-plane present) interlocked in the same chapter, or even on the same page, just made me keep reading the damn thing, waiting for the resolution, which felt obvious, but I couldn't wait to get to it, in a good sense!
King's writing, as always, is brilliant, enticing, catatonic, and any other endearing attribute you may want to give this genius.

And now a rant...
This is the 3rd read that cements the fact that the Jedi just completely and absolutely suck! Their portrayal in [cover:Inquisitor: Rise of the Red Blade|62802781], [b:Dooku: Jedi Lost|44643629|Dooku Jedi Lost (Star Wars)|Cavan Scott|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1553716174l/44643629._SX50_.jpg|69271824], and [b:Padawan|59235877|Padawan (Star Wars)|Kiersten White|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1646880570l/59235877._SY75_.jpg|93387017] shows that they follow their tenets to an extreme that leaves a lot of Padawans lost and unguided, which, makes them look for answers for themselves and has them turn into the Dark Side that allows them to do so. With so many blunders, I would have expected that they would have learned not to disregard someone's questions or doubts, but, alas, here we stand: Padawans left to their demise, while the organization makes them feel excluded and alien, even if they practically kidnapped them at a young age!

Title: O Crime do Padre Amaro
Author: Eça de Queirós
My Review:
Desculpa, Eça, não és tu, sou eu... provavelmente (mas se calhar não)...
Sinto-me mal em dar esta review ao livro, e, ainda mais, sinto-me 'burro' (?) por ser um livro com tanta classificação e a mim ter causado tanto fastio. E, por causa desse sentimento, segue aqui uma review algo extensa para uma má classificação do que senti para com a história.
---
1. Não sou de uma terra pequena, nem tampouco tive contacto com a religião; a isto acresce a falta de descrições do que envolve as personagens (tirando uma ou outra poltrona), e o somatório equivale a algo que, para mim, torna-se impossível de imaginar ou vivenciar.

2. As personagens, na sua grande maioria, são verdadeiramente choninhas e cuscas; talvez a palavra correcta seja 'tristes', porque nunca mostram ânimo verdadeiro e os queixumes são inúmeros e a alegria do 'aqui' e do 'agora' inexistente. Além disso, cheguei ao fim sem saber quem são; talvez não fosse o objectivo, e fossem efectivamente uma matéria cinzenta amorfa que pretende representar apenas o 'estatuto' e 'posição social', mas caiu-me no goto serem todos tão insignificantes

3. Muito pouco, ou mesmo nada, se passa ao longo das 427 páginas que compõem a história; há muito queixume e muita cusquice, mas, a história pareceu-me sempre ausente

4. Faz mais de 10 anos que li Os Maias e na altura senti o mesmo enfado mas assumi que fosse por ser mais novo e decidi dar uma oportunidade ao O Crime do Padre Amaro; a verdade é que o sentimento não mudou - talvez seja pelo estilo realista de Eça, ou talvez por o livro ser antigo e em termos culturais (fora o abuso do poder) ser algo irrelevante, ou talvez seja apenas o meu estilo de leitura e de gosto, mas efectivamente não foi uma boa leitura

Title: Weyward
Author: Emilia Hart
My Review:
With the risk of sounding like a jerk for being a man and poorly reviewing a book about female resilience and empowerment, I'll paraphrase other users' reviews before giving mine.

Look, I'm sorry, I just did not have a good time reading this book. I actually wanted to put it down due to the high volume of confronting content and my own discomfort with it. I was also just not engaged with the characters and frankly, bored. I was somehow both confronted and bored. However I was gifted such a beautiful advance copy, I speed read the second half just so I could form an overall impression.


This book is touted as a female empowering/female resilience type story, but all it really does is put female characters into graphic situations (note: there are many trigger warnings for this book including but not limited to graphic rape, abuse, abortion, deadly injury, persecution, and humiliation/forced nakedness. Then the woman characters deal with that trauma all alone -ahem, not alone, they have their ancestors’ spirits with them- and only one of them ends up with someone by their side in the end…


There are only two men in the book that aren’t villains - one you only see in flashbacks and the other is a bit part mostly seen as a child. The other brutes are atrocious and just as much caricatures as the women - I can’t imagine any man reading this book and seeing any reality in them but it would still seem like an attack to see your gender presented in this way. And to have this book marketed in the way it is - as historical fiction with witchcraft and fantasy elements - is seriously troubling.


Alright, I think that makes the point. Now, my part:
- Having 3 different storylines spread across the time, that are supposed to represent how things don't change, means that you're basically reading the same story 3 times, which is 2 times too much. The book felt extremely long but did not actually provide any value in it, so I ended up bored out of my mind and just trying to rush to the end so I could drop the book.
- I don't know who's responsible for the tags on GoodReads but this is, definitely, NOT historical fiction or even fantasy; basically, nothing really happens except for weird ending arcs that might come across as fantasy
- The synopsis lies... And lies terribly bad... Kate doesn't find her great aunt's secret until the near end and the resolution is lackluster; Altha doesn't use 'all of her powers' to maintain her freedom (most of the time she is just... there...); WWII matters very little for Violet's plot, and, as you can see, very little is written about her in the synopsis
- I enjoyed the way the 3 storylines were written but that just wasn't enough to hold the book until the end

Title: Metro 2033 (Metro, #1)
Author: Dmitry Glukhovsky
My Review:
Four stars pushing into three…
It’s a very difficult book in the sense that it feels like there’s no real connection between moments sometimes. For the first 50% of the book, Artyom felt very passive, and then his personality. just kind of did a 180 turn.
I’m not sure if it’s due to the translation, but several moments felt disconnected from one another; at one moment, you would find the characters sitting down and talking, and in the next moment, they would’ve be in front of a door with no explanation on how or why.
While I enjoyed the scenario and the post apocalyptic way of living, overall, I felt that the first half of the book was just trying to do a lot of worldbuilding for the sake of letting us understand how the world actually existed, but without really providing much value to the plot itself. Not only that, but also Artyom’s revelation felt a bit disconnected from the rest of the story. Although I understand where it comes from, it just felt rushed and without a real purpose to it.
Still giving it four stars due to the originality of the story, and the characters and the world building, but I wouldn’t consider the plot properly good.

My Review:
Gonna be honest... I don't think this book is very good and can't comprehend how there was so much hype around it.
- The world-building is nonexistent (I can't comprehend how there can be a fantasy book without at least properly explaining how it works - and not just 'faes here, humans there, there was a war')
- The writing is way too simple for its own good and even the romance scenes read all the same way
- The plot was very corny for me and I kept thinking of Twilight (maybe this is the Twilight Saga of 2010s); I mean, 'guy kidnaps girl, girl finds out that guy is not that bad, guy and girl fall in love, girl leaves and wants to come back' is not really original
- Amarantha wasn't there to be an interesting character, but it should; it just was portrayed as the generic villain to make the story move forward.

Overall, didn't really make me feel wanting to read the the rest of the books... It's almost like I can guess what will happen on them

My Review:
This book was incredibly boring.

For the first third, I was willing to give 4⭐ because it was edgy and written in a good way but it just kept going on and on and on and ... It never stopped.
The gore and torture ended up being so frequent that I got over it really fast and really didn't do anything for me. It felt too torture-porny and something that you would find during high school and tell others 'Yew, dude, read this!' (you know, like the 2 girls 1 cup thing).

My Review:

The closest I got was 'The book was ok and easy to read" but that doesn't sound like the description of a 5⭐ book, which made me realize that this is, in fact, just an average book (at least for me).

Cons:

Title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
Author: Ken Kesey
Publisher: Blackstone Audio, Inc., and Buck 50 Productions, LLC
My Review:
Definitely not a fan of this book, but I'll consider it average due to its amazing narrative and imagery.

Pros:
- Chief, McMurphy and Big Nurse are well-developed characters and definitely move the story forward
- It opens an argument about how people are treated on mental institutes and how we can do better to make them feel safe and help them
- Also raises eyes to how patients were treated in the 60s and the methodology to deal with them

Cons:
- The book felt outdated to me. I guess that in the 60s it had a lot of power, but, nowadays, it just doesn't have the same impact and you can find multiple examples with the same narrative
- Chief's ramblings / dreams / memories as parallel (I guess) to the way how mental health patients were treated felt dull, long and I found myself just not carrying too much about it and skimming through it
- The racist and misogynistic tone kinda kill the joy for me at times

My Review:

Title: American Gods
Author: Neil Gaiman
Additional Authors: Dennis Boutsikaris, Daniel Oreskes, Ron McLarty, Sarah          Jones
My Review:
If you want characters with personality, make them gods and they’ll put everything out there!
Honestly, that was my favourite part of the book: the personalities; although the gods do like their metaphors, they also enjoy their sharp sense of humour and I think is so ‘easy’ to read thanks to their heavy lifting!

Pros:
- getting to read about all the gods you know of and geek about is like going to a high school reunion but just with the people that you like!
- the story has a good pace to it and although it throws a lot of stuff to you, it doesn’t feel that overwhelming
- the narrator: the type of narrative is just my type of thing - kinda rambling, kinda pointing out the obvious, kinda describing everything that it sees

Cons:
- Part 4 was a bit rough for me; I felt like some conclusions fell into place from nowhere and I think that that’s a common issue with large books - you want to refer to something that happened at the beginning of the story but you need to lean on the chance of the reader to remember it

Definitely gonna read more stuff from Neil Gaiman!

Title: Fairy Tale
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
I think that is my actual first serious read of a King's book and I loved it!
King writes incredibly well and it seems like every word has a proper place in his paragraphs, which still blows my mind.

Pros:
- The book serves as an homage to the great fantasy stories written before and I think it grabs the best parts of each
- King has the ability to introduce just enough characters into the story for it to work and for all of them to have a clear purpose and this book makes that very clear
- I thoroughly enjoyed the world building
- While this book is heavy on the fantasy side, it has its own side of horror, and the balance, for me, is absolutely perfect
- The narrative, descriptions, and dialogues got my attention from start to finish and I didn't feel bored for a single second

Cons:
- Some parts of it felt murky / out of place to me ( like the connection between Charlie's mother's death and his insight on the villain's resolution ) and there were times when I had to go back a few pages to see if I had missed anything

It's definitely my type of story, with my type of writing and my type of narrative!

Title: The Collected Regrets of Clover
Author: Mikki Brammer
My Review:
This beautiful book made me feel miserable since I saw too much of myself in Clover. And that's good because it created a character that showed me I'm not alone.

Pros:
- The story has a good rhythm to it
- The main topic is daring (death) and was definitely treated with respect
- I enjoyed the fact that there was no specific romance in it and the depth of the amorous relationships were murky enough to not be the focus
- You get to learn a bit about the world of death doulas (and also you realize how flawed our worldwide system of dealing with the ones that are passing)
- Although the main topic is dark, the story urges you to enjoy every moment of your life and leaves a beautiful message in it

Cons:
- I wasn't expecting the ending to end as well as it did... Without a perception of time, the resolution and changes in Clover felt too quick
- Some parts felt mundane (which is good) but other parts, mainly the deaths, felt a bit fantastical (as in, time seemed to slow down so everybody could have their happy ending)

Cons:

- the plot is … something …

Overall, a very average book that wins a lot of points by working on a world that a lot of gamers can relate to; but also loses a lot of points for the faulty writing and not very good narrative

Title: The Tattooist of Auschwitz
Author: Heather   Morris
My Review:
I don't like giving books that tackle such horrendous matters such a low rating but this book wasn't good...
At some points (as in, most of the story), while listening to the audiobook, I didn't feel like the setting was a concentration camp. Lale walked freely to pretty much everywhere (even when he wasn't the Tätowierer) and very sparingly noticed the horrors that were happening around him.
I'm sure the real Lale lived horrendous stuff that marked him forever but I personally feel like we were never given a glimpse of that (were the editors too scared of sharing how morbid concentration camps actually were?).

At the end of the book, I just felt like the story romanticizes concentration camps (how is that even possible?) and it felt vague and badly built.

Title: Circe
Author: Madeline Miller
My Review:
As humans, we probably will never understand the stretch of time to which titans, nymphs and gods rule themselves, and that is awesome… but that also means that, if we have a nymph narrating the story, we’ll never have a real grip to the timeframe!
The Song of Achilles hooked me because it was an heroic tale, something that we knew had a finish and it would end badly!
Circe, however, is not an heroic tale. It’s the mundane life of a titan that interacts with humans that come and go.

Pros:
- having a like for Greek mythology and having lived with the Hercules tv show, getting a different view of so many great names is always refreshing
- Miller is extremely good at creating scenarios and making the characters likeable

Cons:
- the last 1/5 of the book felt rushed and didn’t seem to fit with the rest
- I personally feel like there were parts that were extremely detailed and others that were just waved at
- It’s not the most captivating story

Sadly I give it a 3⭐️because it just wasn’t very entertaining

- The story about a scientist, who discovered how to create clones, and now lives in the moral dilemma on how similar she should make them similar to their own humane counterparts
- The story about that same scientist and how her husband ended up betraying her to do his own research just to create a clone of her

- The story of a scientist, trying to reproduce the best way, possible, his wife or her wife, and completely failing it, and having a garden full of dead bad clones

Title: The Song of Achilles
Author: Madeline Miller
My Review:
I need to split my review with 3 different views on it.

---

This is not a book for hardcore Greek mythology fans. It is a romanticized version of the Iliad, and it is a beautiful one. You will find mismatches with the Iliad but I advise you to ignore them and read the book for what it is: a book with a good story.

---

Reading this book was like getting together with old friends! If you've watched 90's Hercules (movie and tv show), you'll find a lot of recognizable characters, and that's precisely what happened to me! After 20+ years, I was again reunited with heroes, foes, and thinkers that I've exhaustively read and watched throughout my childhood!

---

It is a beautifully written book with a good romance in it. It shows how cruel life can be and how dangerous one's ambitions are. If you're not a fan of Greek Mythology, the names will bore you and you'll exasperate over the need of being 'remembered for honour'; but if you're slightly inclined to it, you'll find a good book!

Title: The Maidens
Author: Alex Michaelides
My Review:

It reads like a beautiful poem (it's very atmospheric) but lacks a lot of sustenance!
The characters look and sound flat and are incredibly stereotypical.

Also, you can't call it a mystery/thriller just because you have your main character following the red herring the entire time.

About the audiobook: Louise Brealey's narration was very good and her calm voice certainly helped to create a certain ambiance (maybe that was the only thing salvaging the book!).
Certainly, not a fan of the book but will surely hear more stuff from Brealey!

Having back-and-forths on the timelines (and between two different characters) ended up making me feel completely detached from the story.

It wasn't a particularly pleasant reading...

Title: Roadside Picnic
Author: Arkady Strugatsky
Additional Authors: Boris Strugatsky, Theodore Sturgeon, Antonina W. Bouis
My Review:
SF for me needs to be confusing, rash, and direct, and Roadside Picnic delivers just that.
It doesn't delve deep into technological descriptions because our main character, Red, isn't interested in that; it doesn't explore the current political panorama because Red, once again, isn't affected by it.
Our main character lives his own life and we reach the end with a true climax of his personality and place in the world.

It's not often that you get to read something that made a huge mark in history, but here is Roadside Picnic, doing just that.

I just wished it was a little bit longer so I could find more about the world

My Review:
If I'm going to be honest, reading 'Atomic Habits' felt somewhat like a chore since it ended up evocating a lot of stuff that I previously read online or saw threads on Twitter about. I didn't feel the need to take notes with this book since there weren't any new insights for me.

However, I believe it offers strong insights for anyone who hasn't been in touch with the topic. It has good strategies in it and offers a nice framework for people to implement in their lives.

That being said, my rating reflects the lack of value that I was able to take from the book compared to previous sources

Honestly, the book lost me a bit in the middle but it's not possible not to love Poirot, especially since the story starts fully with him (and a marvelous interaction between narrator and Poirot).

It pains me to say this but this is a very underwhelming book. The plot seems bleak and sort of made of at the end and story itself felt … ‘weird’!

My Review:
Definitely a strange book but I don’t really know what to say about it. At the end it just felt like a regular creepy pasta.
Maybe there was some sort of metaphor that you’re supposed to get but I really couldn’t get much out of it

Title: Win, Lose or Die (John Gardner's Bond, #8)
Author: John  Gardner
My Review:
I very, very, very poor book.
I can forgive how corny it feels since it is an old book but it just feels like it's poorly written with the story dragging along for what seems forever.
I have another Bond book by Gardner... Let's see if that one is any better.

Title: Among the Beasts & Briars
Author: Ashley Poston
My Review:
I feel bad for giving it 2 stars, but I couldn't connect with it.
The descriptions felt bleaks (and repetitive) most of the time and the dialogues between characters didn't really feel natural to me. The plot is kinda meh and seemed unfinished, with a lot of points that just were passed by without much attention to it, and the "action" in it was also very flat.
The story also felt extremely slow and I ended up listening to it at 2x.

It has a lot of potential but it ended up being very underwhelming.

Author: George Orwell
My Review:
This is my first Orwell and possibly won’t be the last.
His writing is entertaining and his topics extremely pertinent and it’s easy to do the correlation with our own lives.
I suggest at least giving it a chance

While the plot feels a bit thin in some places, the characters' interactions make up for it.

I would like to give it 5 stars but the story felt rushed once I got to the middle of the book.

Title: Neuromancer (Sprawl, #1)
Author: William Gibson
My Review:
Once I finished 'Neuromancer' I went to my phone and Googled 'Neuromancer is confusing' and I started seeing what people were saying about it.

I was ready to give this book a bad rating because I couldn't understand most of it but then it struck me: the story is being told from Case's (the main character) POV and that means that I wasn't going to get a deep description of everything around him (technologies, jargon and so on) because he was already familiar with it. That ended up intriguing me...
I'm used to having a character tell me everything I need to know about a scene but that's not very realistic. The characters wouldn't end up hovering over every single detail because they would be familiar with most of it and that's what makes Neuromancer different.

Neuromancer throws you right at the thick of it and expects you to just go with it. You learn as you go. There are expressions and words that you'll never know what they are but that's what's great about Science Fiction: you can create your own ideas based on what the author wrote!

The book doesn't get 5 stars from me because it does what I wrote above TOO WELL. I had a hard time grasping what was going around me and I finished the book feeling confused and disoriented...

But I also had the feeling of wanting to read it again just so I could better understand its world!

And that means that it was a fantastic book!

Title: Convenience Store Woman
Author: Sayaka Murata
My Review:
The active voice of the book is Keiko, a character that doesn't understand many social cues.
This ends up being the book's demise because:
- it doesn't allow itself to be the critique to conformity that it wants to be (because Keiko doesn't fully understand what this means)
- Keiko's personality is waved off as being 'quirky' (which is not and should be treated as such)
- it tries to make a commentary on work culture (and how you get praised for disregarding your personal life), but, again, since we're reading from a non-neurotypical character point of view, it never presents itself as something bad

There's not much to say about the book. There is no plot and it's incredibly mundane (not in a good way).
The convenience store scenario ends up being the most interesting part because it showcases the neatly organized products, the Chorei routine, and a bit of Japan's work culture.

Maybe it just wasn't the book for me

Title: Calamity Town (Ellery Queen Detective, #16)
Author: Ellery Queen
My Review:
It is a well-written murder mystery that pretty much has everything that you would expect from the genre.
Descriptive and easy to read, you go from one page to another without noticing.
There are times, tho, where you don't really know which character is speaking since the dialogues don't have cues to it, but, other than that, entertaining.

Title: Secrets of the Millionaire Mind: Mastering the Inner Game of Wealth
Author: T. Harv Eker
My Review:
If you're interested in this book to know the 'secret recipe' for being rich, you'll be extremely disappointed.

While the premise of the book is very good (change your way of thinking to be able to see things differently), it overextends it by going through the 'positive thinking' and 'the universe is not against you'. If you can look past that, it has some great insights and will most probably change your life in a good way (and that's all we can ask about, really).

However... My bad score for this book lands on the fact that:
- the good points could be listed on a 10-minute read instead of 212 pages
- the premise on why I should listen to Harv is because he has seminars about being rich
- most of the book is about changing your habits and way of thinking but rephrased in different ways

The book gets salvaged by:
- several insight moments (that means, you end up seeing a lot of stuff written that you might have thought but never really stopped to take a closer look at it)
- offers a different point of view that some people might not be used to

I feel bad for giving this book a bad score because it's pretty much against what Harv 'teaches' and some of his stuff is pretty much accurate but I feel like there are better books out there with more complete information and with a clear learning path

Title: The Bishop Murder Case (A Philo Vance Mystery #4)
Author: S.S. Van Dine
My Review:
It's not great. It's not bad. It's just another mystery novel.

To be absolutely frank, most of the book doesn't actually explore and investigate the murder. It just keeps adding more and more details that seem to only exist to fill pages.

I'm not a fan of books where you're able to find the culprit before or even at the same time as the main character and, sadly, this is one of those cases.

Compared to other mystery novels, this book doesn't add much to anything, which is a pity.
